newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Net profit tumbles at Norway's UBN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Net profit tumbles at Norway's UBN.

text.p: Union Bank of Norway, the country's biggest savings bank, said on Thursday that higher costs and lower interest margins led to a 21 percent drop in net profits.

UBN reported net profit of 851 million crowns ($128.2 million), down from 1.07 billion in 1995. After tax, and a provision of 155 million crowns for reorganisation measures, the return on equity was 13.8 percent.
Operating profit before losses came to 1.13 billion, down from 1.43 billion crowns, while pre-tax operating profit dropped to 1.17 billion from 1.41 billion.

Banks president Kjell Kran said he was pleased with the profits given the tough competition in overbanked Norway, but said he expected this year's result to be somewhat weaker partly due to narrowing interest margins.
"I expect Union Bank of Norway's 1997 financial result to be somewhat weaker," he said.

"Excess capacity in the market will probably result in the customer spread falling also in 1997. Nor can we expect such abormal loss figures this year. In spite of this, 1997 should produce a good financial result."
The board proposed the dividend be unchanged at 15 crowns per primary capital certificate, a hybrid share.
The result was roughly in line with market expectations and UBN shares closed 0.2 percent lower at 211 crowns on the Oslo Bourse.
Operating costs rose to 2.98 billion crowns from 2.65 billion mainly because of the purchase of new subsidiaries, development costs and provisions for staff cuts and restructuring.
The bank, known locally as Sparebanken NOR, said the average margin fell to 2.9 percent at the end of 1996 from 3.5 percent at the end of 1995.
"Competition in the market is growing constantly, and has resulted in the bank's margins being considerably narrower," a statement said.
Net interest income fell to 2.56 billion crowns from 2.78 billion. But loan volume continued positively with 12-month growth of 14 percent, up from 10 percent in 1995.

"A substantial growth in volumes, particularly for loans to business customers, higher income from subsidiaries and net recoveries on loan losses had a positive impact on the group result," the bank said.

Despite higher lending volume, Norwegian banks are suffering from lower net interest income, their core business. Shrinking interest margins are forcing them to prioritise other means of income, analysts say.

Other operating income at UBN rose to 1.55 billion crowns from 1.30 billion in 1995 due to an increase in the use of money transfer services and higher income from the sale of products by subsidiaries such as the group's insurance company NOR Forsikring.
"Over several years we have systematically worked for developments which make us less vulnerable to decreasing spreads in the bank's core business," Kran said.
